tagline: Peach orchards and villages give way to the Blue Ridge foothills
intro: SC 11 links peach orchards and villages with the Blue Ridge foothills, crossing rolling country in Cherokee and Spartanburg counties. The Federal Highway Administration presents the Cherokee Foothills National Scenic Byway as a two-lane drive past Cowpens National Battlefield and over Lake Keowee. Its listing gives 112 miles and three hours of driving. Mountain views along the corridor include Table Rock, Caesars Head and Glassy.

FHWA traces the corridor to an older Cherokee path. The numbered highway also absorbed newer road segments: most of SC 112 between New Prospect and Chesnee became part of SC 11 in 1939. National Scenic Byway designation followed in 1998, making the route eligible for federal improvement and enhancement funds. State law names SC 11 the Cherokee Foothills Scenic Highway while retaining Andrew Pickens Scenic Parkway for its Pickens and Oconee county portion.

From I-85 at Gaffney, head west past Cowpens and through Chesnee toward Campobello. Near Cleveland, SC 11 shares US 276, the road that reaches Caesars Head. Continue toward Table Rock and the Lake Keowee bridges. West Union offers a turn toward neighboring Walhalla before the highway continues south to I-85 near Georgia. Here the byway returns to the interstate after its arc through the foothills of northern South Carolina.

moments.title: Cowpens National Battlefield
moments.text: Daniel Morgan’s victory over Banastre Tarleton on January 17, 1781, is the central story at Cowpens. The National Park Service preserves the Revolutionary War battlefield just east of Chesnee. Established as a national battlefield site in 1929, Cowpens transferred from the War Department in 1933 and received its present designation in 1972. A walking tour follows the field, while the visitor-center museum places the battle within the war’s Southern Campaign using a fiber-optic map. A reconstructed log cabin represents another chapter of the land’s use: Robert Scruggs farmed here before the park was established.
moments.notice: The Scruggs log cabin is a reconstruction of the home associated with a farmer who preceded the park.

moments.title: Caesars Head
moments.text: The granitic gneiss outcrop at Caesars Head stands 3,208 feet above sea level on the Blue Ridge Escarpment. Reached by US 276, the site had a hotel and cottages before it became state parkland. The hotel, a cottage and the original Hagood house burned in September 1954. South Carolina’s parks department acquired the land from several owners between 1976 and 1986. The park has panoramic mountain views, and each autumn it becomes a seasonal home for thousands of migrating hawks. The headquarters visitor center displays photographs of the park’s human history and a relief map of the Mountain Bridge Wilderness Area.
moments.notice: The rock outcrop overlooks the Piedmont from the Blue Ridge Escarpment.

moments.title: Walhalla
moments.text: Walhalla’s name reaches into Norse mythology, but its founding was a nineteenth-century immigration project. The German Colonization Society of Charleston formed in 1848 to help immigrants following the failed German revolutions of 1848–1849. Its trustees bought land in December 1849, and the city was founded in 1850. Walhalla became Oconee County’s seat in 1868. The city’s annual Oktoberfest continues the German connection with music, dancing and food on Sertoma Field. The 1901 Walhalla Graded School has another civic role now: the historic school building is used as the Walhalla Civic Auditorium.
